# Escape hatches, one at a time

Zig has no `unsafe` keyword, so "no unsafe code" needs a definition before
it means anything. Here it is: **no operation that can reinterpret memory,
bypass a runtime check, or read uninitialised storage** -- except at a
boundary that cannot be expressed otherwise, justified individually.

Counting them answers *how many*, which is the weaker question. This page
answers *which ones, and why is each sound*.

```sh
make safety                                   # budget gate + this inventory
python3 scripts/safety-inventory.py --self-test
```

**59 occurrences in the shipped library, 0 unclassified.**
5 more live in `test` blocks, which never reach the archive.

## Never present

These are not budgeted at some small number; they are absent, and the check
fails if one appears.

| Operation | Count |
| --- | --- |
| `@constCast` | 0 |
| `@setRuntimeSafety` | 0 |
| `asm` | 0 |
| `unreachable` | 0 |
| `volatile` | 0 |

Force-unwraps (`.?`) are also zero, enforced by the budget gate in
[`scripts/safety-scan.sh`](../scripts/safety-scan.sh).

A caveat that matters: comment text is stripped before scanning, so prose
*about* `unreachable` in `DECISIONS.md` or a doc comment does not count as a
use of it. The self-test covers exactly that case, and the reverse -- a `//`
inside a string literal must not swallow the rest of the line.

## What is present, by category

### c-allocator-boundary (8)

`json_allocator` is a C interface: `malloc`/`realloc`/`free` speak `void*`. Every crossing needs a cast, and each one round-trips a pointer back to the same element type it went in as. None reinterprets one object type as another.

> The container stack round-trips through the C allocator's void*. Going in it is a [*]Stack; coming out it is re-typed to the same element type, never to a different one.

| [`src/parser.zig:257`](../src/parser.zig#L257) | `push` | `@ptrCast` | `self.stack = @ptrCast(@alignCast(p));` |

> The token buffer round-trips through the C allocator as void*, back to [*]u8 with alignment 1.

| Location | Function | Operation | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`src/parser.zig:324`](../src/parser.zig#L324) | `pushcharSlow` | `@ptrCast` | `const p = cRealloc(self, @ptrCast(self.data.string), size) ...` |
| [`src/parser.zig:329`](../src/parser.zig#L329) | `pushcharSlow` | `@ptrCast` | `self.data.string = @ptrCast(p);` |

> Releasing the stack and the token buffer through free(), which takes void*. Both pointers came from this allocator.

| Location | Function | Operation | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

> json_allocator.malloc is a C interface returning void*. The result is immediately treated as [*]u8, whose alignment is 1, so no alignment assumption is made. A null return is handled by the caller as OOM.

> C requires realloc's result to be suitably aligned for any object type with a fundamental alignment, which includes struct json_stack. This states that guarantee to the compiler; it is checked at runtime in ReleaseSafe, which is the mode this library ships.

`@intCast` is *checked* in ReleaseSafe. A bound that turned out to be wrong aborts loudly rather than corrupting memory. That the bounds hold on untrusted input is evidence from fuzzing, not an assertion made here.

### deliberate-wraparound (14)

The opposite of an escape hatch: these *add* definition. C's counters are unsigned and allowed to wrap, and the empty-stack sentinel is `(size_t)-1` reached by decrementing 0. Using `+%`/`-%` rather than `+`/`-` is what stops untrusted input from turning an overflow into a panic.

> C's counters are unsigned and allowed to wrap; source.position, lineno and ntokens must therefore wrap rather than panic, or untrusted input could take down the process. stack_top's increment past the (size_t)-1 empty sentinel depends on it.

| Location | Function | Operation | Source |

| [`src/parser.zig:688`](../src/parser.zig#L688) | `readValue` | `+%` | `self.ntokens +%= 1;` |

### public-header-boundary (3)

The pinned header promises `char*` and takes `const void*`. These are the header's own contract, not a choice this port made.

> The pinned header declares the parameter const void*, so the cast to [*]const u8 is the header's own contract. The length is taken from the caller's size argument and never derived from the pointer.

### write-before-read (2)

Storage fully written before anything reads it back.

> The json_stream is handed straight to core.openBuffer, which fills every field, on the next line. Nothing reads it in between, and the value does not escape until after.

## Why occurrences are keyed by function, not by line

The previous report listed `parser.zig:1011`. By the time anyone read it the
line was 1018, because seven lines had been inserted above it and nothing
re-derived the file. A justification pinned to a line number rots silently,
and a rotted justification is worse than none -- it reads as verified.

So every rule is keyed by `(file, enclosing function, operation)`. Line
numbers are still recorded, because they are useful for navigation, but they
are not what the justification hangs on.

Some rules use a wildcard function (`*`) where the reason genuinely does not
vary between sites -- every `@intCast` in `strtod.zig` is the same argument.
Where a wildcard turned out to cover two different things it was split:
`api.zig`'s `= undefined` rule described the parser's own state and was
silently being applied to a *test*'s scratch array. That is what motivated
separating test blocks out, and the self-test now pins the behaviour.

## An unclassified occurrence fails the build

A budget with room in it absorbs a new escape hatch without comment. A rule
table does not: a hatch at a site the table does not know about is reported
as `unclassified` and `make safety` exits non-zero. Introducing one is then
a deliberate edit to
[`scripts/safety-inventory.py`](../scripts/safety-inventory.py), which shows
up in review.

## The classifier is itself tested

Ten cases, each one a way this analysis could quietly report the wrong thing:
a forbidden operation not being flagged, a hatch at a new site inheriting an
existing justification, a mention in a comment being counted as a use, `//`
inside a string literal swallowing a cast, `->` being read as a wrapping
subtract, two hatches on one line counting as one, a test block's scratch
being counted as shipped code.

```
$ python3 scripts/safety-inventory.py --self-test
self-test: 10 cases, 0 failure(s)
```

## Limits, stated plainly

- **These are arguments, not proofs.** Each justification says why an
  operation is sound; none is machine-checked. What *is* machine-checked is
  that every occurrence has one, that none is forbidden, and that the
  inventory matches the current source.
- **Scope is `src/`.** The tools in `tools/` and the harnesses are not
  scanned; they are not shipped.
- **It is textual.** A hatch reached through a construct the scanner does
  not model -- `@call` with a builtin name assembled at comptime, say --
  would be missed. Nothing in this codebase does that.
- **`@intCast` bounds are argued, not proven.** The claim that they hold on
  untrusted input rests on the fuzz session and the random-input regression
  test, and is only as strong as that evidence.
